Welcome, Garrett.
Thank you, and good afternoon, Mayor and Council.
It's my pleasure this afternoon to present to you Kitchener's allocation policy and bylaw,
which is our measured response to the ongoing water capacity constraint period in the Mannheim service area.
So Council will recall that the city has launched the incident management team
as a way to manage and coordinate the City of Kitchener's response to this issue.
The water allocation policy is a large body of work that was contributed to by many people on that team.
City of Kitchener staff, in consultation with other area municipalities, the development industry,
and really staff from across the organization have worked together to deliver this work.
That includes staff from engineering, building, planning and housing policy, DSDGM's office,
INS, GM, Office, Communications, Development and Housing Approvals, Planning and Housing
Policy, Kitchener Utilities, Finance, Emergency Management and Business Continuity, Legal
CAO's Office and all of CLT.
So I am pleased and it's a pleasure to present this work today on behalf of that entire larger
body of work and that larger team.
Kitchener is well positioned today to advance our water allocation policy in advance of
the first water allocation from the region which is anticipated very soon.
There will be water allocation moving forward based on the risk-based management framework
that's been approved by the region, as well as a one-time increase in allocation in the coming weeks
as part of some well-optimization work that's being done by the region.
We anticipate to get formal confirmation of what that water capacity could be by the end of this week
or early next week, and it's imperative that we move forward with water allocation policy and bylaw
so that we are in a position to be able to then transfer that water capacity allocation to the industry
to support housing, economic development, and job growth.
This policy is intended to guide and prioritize for the city's use of water capacity allocation
and that in an interim period where there is a capacity constraint,
the city will apply a prioritization criteria which aligns with strategic priorities of council,
including supporting affordable housing as well as economic development and job growth.
It is a transparent process through a bylaw and an attached policy
that has been designed to continue to meet the city's evolving needs
during this capacity constraint period.
We are proposing a new process that we've worked with the industry to develop.
Ultimately, this additional step is of no cost,
and it's as simple as filling out a form,
which allows us to be able to understand what our current and upcoming water capacity demand needs will be
and allows us to forecast between now and 2031 where we know that we're going to have to apply this policy in some form
moving forward until we're completely out of the constraint period.
That application form will be reviewed in conjunction with the concurrent development application.
So it's not a linear process. This is something we're doing in parallel.
is not intended to add any cost or time to a development application.
Water allocation will be provided by the City of Kitchener in one of two ways.
One either through a water allocation letter, which confirms that the water capacity is available,
allowing a development to proceed.
The second is through a forward-looking servicing agreement,
which would be a City of Kitchener commitment to ensure that we reserve future water capacity
at the appropriate quarter for when a development may come online.
The latter has been designed so that we know we have some developments in the city that take longer to construct.
A high-rise building, as an example, can start construction in several years away from occupancy.
We listened to the industry, and they wanted a clear path forward so they'd be able to advance construction in advance of final water allocation.
We know each quarter we're going to be further away from a water capacity constraint issue,
and this allows development to continue and aligns when that water will be delivered with when the developments will come online.
There's been significant engagement on this particular issue since December of 2025.
Staff have responded to over 700 emails, have been part of 30 site-specific meetings.
There was a neighbourhood information meeting held on Zoom on June 11th where the development
industry both our larger development industry organizations and representations as well as
the smaller developers attended.
There were some follow-up meetings from that, and then last week there was a meeting with
the Waterloo Region Home Builders Association where we went line by line through the policy
and offered explanations and made some amendments that are outlined in the staff report.
We have, it's important to note that while we've engaged formally with development organizations
including Build Urban and Waterloo Region Home Builders Association, we also have maintained
constant contact and updates with some of our smaller builders that do some of the smaller
projects.
So we have incorporated feedback within the policy and the bylaw and is intended to be
implemented through a zoning bylaw which amends both of our zoning bylaws which allows us
to implement the policy as applicable law into the Billnico.
So that is a very brief summary of the last six months and how this has been developed
and I'm pleased to answer any questions.

Great aqueducts and Romanesque baths across the globe, which were a

responsibility to appropriate technical staff, in this case the general manager of the development

average resident. Transparency is paramount to public trust. It reinforces confidence in
decision-making and allows for a data-driven perspective to support understanding.
